title: Mu-qt-PEGASIS: Interactive Aggregate Signatures from Effective Isogenies in the Programmable Random-Oracle Model
authors: Nouhou Abdou Idris and Mustapha Hedabou
abstract:
We present Mu-qt-PEGASIS, a mathematically precise con-
ditional compiler for interactive aggregate signatures built from the
qt-PEGASIS effective class-group action. Our central observation is that
the torsor structure of the public-key space blocks the standard Schnorr-
or BLS-style verification equations used in conventional aggregate sig-
natures. We resolve this by separating verification into two layers: a
proof-authentication layer that certifies public-key registration and round-
robin key aggregation, and a transcript-consistency layer that verifies the
final aggregate signature relative to an authenticated aggregate key.
The resulting framework is formulated in the programmable random-oracle
model. Public-key registration and linked aggregation are authenticated
via Fiat–Shamir compilations of explicit public-coin Σ-protocols for the
relations Rreg and Rlink . Under the hardness of the Group Action Inverse
Problem (GAIP), together with the random-oracle assumptions for Hnizk
and Hsig , we prove MU-EUF-CMA security against static corruptions.
At the protocol level, for a fixed Fiat–Shamir repetition parameter t, the
aggregate signature has size O(t) and is independent of the number of
signers n, while the authenticated registration and aggregation transcript
remain linear in n.

      Abstract. We present Mu-qt-PEGASIS, a mathematically precise con-
      ditional compiler for interactive aggregate signatures built from the
      qt-PEGASIS effective class-group action. Our central observation is that
      the torsor structure of the public-key space blocks the standard Schnorr-
      or BLS-style verification equations used in conventional aggregate sig-
      natures. We resolve this by separating verification into two layers: a
      proof-authentication layer that certifies public-key registration and round-
      robin key aggregation, and a transcript-consistency layer that verifies the
      final aggregate signature relative to an authenticated aggregate key.
      The resulting framework is formulated in the programmable random-oracle
      model. Public-key registration and linked aggregation are authenticated
      via Fiat–Shamir compilations of explicit public-coin Σ-protocols for the
      relations Rreg and Rlink . Under the hardness of the Group Action Inverse
      Problem (GAIP), together with the random-oracle assumptions for Hnizk
      and Hsig , we prove MU-EUF-CMA security against static corruptions.
      At the protocol level, for a fixed Fiat–Shamir repetition parameter t, the
      aggregate signature has size O(t) and is independent of the number of
      signers n, while the authenticated registration and aggregation transcript
      remain linear in n.

1    Introduction

Aggregate signatures enable multiple independently generated signatures to be
compressed into a single succinct object whose validity can be verified collectively.
Since the seminal work of Boneh, Gentry, Lynn, and Shacham (BGLS) over
bilinear pairings [2], aggregate signatures have become a fundamental primitive
in modern public-key cryptography, with applications to certificate transparency,
authenticated distributed systems, blockchain protocols, secure routing, and
bandwidth-constrained communication.
2       F. Author et al.

     Nearly all existing aggregate-signature constructions rely on an explicit al-
gebraic operation over public keys or signatures. Pairing-based schemes exploit
bilinearity, Schnorr-type multisignatures use the additive group law of discrete
logarithm groups, and lattice-based approaches similarly aggregate algebraic
objects through publicly computable linear operations. The existence of such
an efficiently computable public combiner is therefore an implicit structural
assumption underlying essentially every known aggregation paradigm.
     Recent advances in effective class-group actions have established a new family
of post-quantum cryptographic primitives based on the action of ideal class
groups on superspecial abelian varieties. Beginning with CSIDH [9] and continuing
through PEGASIS [10] and qt-PEGASIS [11], these constructions provide efficient
effective group actions while avoiding the algebraic structures exploited by
quantum algorithms against discrete logarithms and pairings. Consequently, they
constitute an attractive foundation for post-quantum public-key cryptography.
     However, effective group actions differ fundamentally from classical group-
based cryptography. Although the acting class group is algebraically well defined,
its elements are intentionally hidden, and only their action on public orbit elements
is efficiently computable. As a consequence, there is no efficiently computable
binary operation on public keys analogous to group multiplication or addition.
This raises a fundamental question:
    Can aggregate signatures be constructed over effective class-group actions
    using the same aggregation paradigm that underlies BLS, MuSig, and
    related schemes?
    The first contribution of this paper is to show that, in general, the answer is
negative.
    We prove that any generic public combiner capable of aggregating indepen-
dently generated public keys over effective class-group actions would yield an
efficient algorithm for recovering hidden class-group elements, thereby violat-
ing the underlying hardness assumption. Thus, unlike in pairing- or discrete-
logarithm-based cryptography, public aggregation is not merely absent from
existing constructions—it is provably incompatible with the security assumptions
underlying effective group actions.
    This impossibility result identifies the precise obstruction preventing the direct
adaptation of classical aggregate-signature techniques to the qt-PEGASIS setting.
Rather than viewing the lack of a public group operation as an implementation
inconvenience, we show that it represents a fundamental cryptographic limitation.
    Having identified this obstruction, we develop a new aggregation framework
that circumvents it. Instead of aggregating public keys algebraically, we authen-
ticate each individual class-group action by means of explicit witness-linking
proofs. Aggregation is therefore performed over authenticated action transcripts
rather than over public keys themselves. This yields a modular compiler trans-
forming independently generated effective class-group actions into authenticated
aggregate signatures.
    To instantiate the proof layer concretely, we construct public-coin Σ-protocols
for both registration and witness linkage and compile them via the Fiat–Shamir
                                                         Mu-qt-PEGASIS          3

transform in the programmable random-oracle model. The resulting aggregate-
signature scheme enjoys a complete MU-EUF-CMA security proof under the
Group Action Inversion Problem (GAIP), while remaining fully compatible with
the qt-PEGASIS effective class-group action.
    Finally, we implement the complete construction in SageMath using the
qt-PEGASIS arithmetic at the 500-bit CSURF parameter level. Although the
implementation is intended as a proof-of-concept rather than a fully optimized
realization, the experimental evaluation confirms the correctness of the construc-
tion, validates its asymptotic behavior, and demonstrates that the aggregate
signature remains independent of the number of signers for fixed Fiat–Shamir
parameters.

Our Contributions. The principal contributions of this work are summarized
below.

 – We identify a fundamental obstruction to aggregate signatures over effective
   class-group actions by proving that any generic public aggregation algorithm
   would violate the underlying hardness assumption.
 – We introduce the first authenticated interactive aggregate-signature frame-
   work specifically designed for qt-PEGASIS effective class-group actions.
 – We construct explicit witness-linking and registration Σ-protocols together
   with their Fiat–Shamir compilation in the programmable random-oracle
   model.
 – We prove MU-EUF-CMA security of the resulting aggregate-signature scheme
   via a reduction to the Group Action Inversion Problem.
 – We implement the complete protocol and experimentally evaluate its per-
   formance, communication costs, and scalability on top of the qt-PEGASIS
   reference implementation.

    More broadly, our results suggest that aggregate signatures over effective
group actions require a fundamentally different design philosophy from their
classical counterparts. Rather than relying on explicit algebraic aggregation,
secure post-quantum aggregation can instead be achieved through authenticated
proofs of action consistency.

5     Barrier to Non-interactive Aggregation
In classical aggregate-signature constructions, aggregation is enabled by a public
algebraic rule that combines independently generated public objects into a single
verification identity. In BLS-type systems this rule is induced by bilinearity, while
in Schnorr-type systems it is induced by the public group law on the verification
key space [1,2]. In our setting, by contrast, the public-key space Xp (O) is a torsor
under Cl(O) rather than a publicly represented group. Consequently, there is no
a priori public operation on orbit elements with respect to which one could write
an aggregation equation of the form used in classical schemes.
    The purpose of this section is to formalize this obstruction. We show that the
existence of a sufficiently strong public combiner on orbit elements would force
Xp (O) itself to inherit an efficiently computable abelian group law. Once this
happens, the map

                ϕX0 : Cl(O) −→ Xp (O),          ϕX0 ([a]) := [a] ∗ X0 ,

ceases to behave merely as a hidden-action parametrization of a torsor and
becomes an efficiently computable group isomorphism onto a public group. Quan-
tum algorithms for finite abelian groups can then be used to invert ϕX0 efficiently,
contradicting Assumption 1.

5.1   The combiner abstraction
We isolate the natural algebraic functionality that a non-interactive aggregate-
signature construction would need in order to combine independently generated
public keys directly at the level of orbit elements.

Definition 3 (Combiner). Fix a base point X0 ∈ Xp (O). A combiner is a
polynomial-time algorithm

                           Comb : Xp (O) × Xp (O) → Xp (O)

11    Conclusion

Mu-qt-PEGASIS isolates the precise proof-theoretic ingredient needed to obtain

Definition 7 (Group action). Let (G, ◦) be a group with identity e ∈ G, and
let X be a set. A map

is a group action if e ⋆ x = x for all x ∈ X , and (g ◦ h) ⋆ x = g ⋆ (h ⋆ x) for all

Definition 8 (Effective group action, EGA [24, Def. 3],[25]). A group
action (G, X , ⋆) is an effective group action (EGA) if

 1. G is finite, and there are efficient algorithms for membership testing, equality

 2. X is finite, and there are efficient algorithms for membership testing and for
    computing a unique representation of each element;
 3. there is a distinguished element x̃ ∈ X with known representation, called the
    origin;
 4. there is an efficient algorithm to evaluate the action, i.e. to compute g ⋆ x
    given g ∈ G and x ∈ X .

We write (G, X , ⋆, x̃) for an EGA.

attention throughout to EGAs of known order, since (a) the security of a group
action must not rest on secrecy of the group structure of G, and (b) this is the
regime in which Cl(O)-actions such as CSIDH, PEGASIS and qt-PEGASIS are
deployed once the class number and a generator have been computed [27].
